text: Embedding gallery browse, on PE-Core-L14: it matches by artist, not by image. "Seems to consider 'close' artworks when they are by the same artist, even if the images themselves don't look much alike (happens for toxicity, johns, krafty, muse, infected). For some of them it could be the band's logo that is the same, for others it might be the textual content that is the same (band's name), or it has deep knowledge of music artworks."
Embedding gallery browse, DINOv2 vs DINOv3 attend to different structure: "For krafty, DINOv2 focused on the layout and flowers, while DINOv3 seems to have focused more on the strong typography."

Embedding gallery browse, DINOv3 sometimes matches semantic category across styles: "For the boat in johns -> a picture of a boat, a painting of a boat, a logo of a boat, a drawing of an origami boat, all in different styles but all boats."
Embedding gallery browse, overall: "I think the DINO models are better, but I wouldn't know which one of the 2."
SAM mask review: "sometimes 'logo' could be part of the artwork itself, or some sort of added branding" — and likewise "sticker": part of the artwork, or something added on top.
SAM mask review: "i did not count 'parental advisory' marks as 'stickers' but the model seemed to consider them as stickers."
SAM mask review, on faces firing on depicted faces: "a graffiti of a face", "a sculpted bust".
SAM mask review: "a chinese character was recognized as a word (not incorrect, just interesting)".
SAM mask review: album-title masks sometimes ambiguous between the title and the artist name — "definitely some of the main text".
SAM mask review, on the overlay rendering (mask fill + bbox + locator ring): "the three-layer rendering was helpful in some cases, i just got confused the first time that's all."

Premise disambiguation round, canonical ruling: ground_type has a gap for "one flat field + one shaded field with a blurry meeting line". The test is surface identity, never boundary softness — one surface partly flat / partly shaded is shaded_field; two areas with a soft join are multiple_distinct_fields; genuine 5-second ambiguity is answered on the gut read, because the forced choice has to be symmetric with the VLM's.

Premise disambiguation round, second canonical ruling: one wall painted in bands that melt into each other is shaded_field — the contract's genuine three-stop gradient case; the same wall in crisp bands is multiple_distinct_fields. The axis is whether the ground reads as one continuous color progression or as discrete color areas; surface identity is a strong prior, neither necessary nor sufficient.

Adjudication browse: the published gradient flag is palette-conditional, not an artwork label. "The flat/gradient flag might not be the most fair comparison since it can really depend on which colors were picked for background/surface too." An artwork can support a valid flat palette and a valid gradient palette; the flag records which choice won. The reviewer also reported that where they voted differently from the oracle, they could see its point of view.

No axis covers instrument behaviour. The nearest words (provenance/overlay-color-ignored, identity/signature-color-missing) are all about a colour that reached or missed a role, which is not what the reviewer is talking about.
VOCABULARY GAP: a comparison of what two embedding models attend to (layout/flowers vs typography). Nothing in the vocabulary can express "instrument A attends to X, instrument B attends to Y".
VOCABULARY GAP: an observation that a model groups by semantic category across visual styles. No tag for cross-style semantic matching.

VOCABULARY GAP: an overall preference between two instruments, with the reviewer unable to separate the two finalists. meta/sides-indistinguishable is the closest wording ("the two sides look the same to the reviewer; the comparison carries no information") but "sides" in this vocabulary means the two palettes of one pairwise item, so using it here would be an approximation. Flagged unsure so a human can decide whether the meta axis is meant to be scope-free.

VOCABULARY GAP: the reviewer is questioning whether "logo"/"sticker" are provenance categories at all (part of the artwork vs added on top). The provenance axis can only say that a *published colour* came from an overlay; it cannot record a statement about the overlay-vs-material distinction itself.

VOCABULARY GAP: a mismatch between the reviewer's category and the model's label word (parental-advisory marks counted as stickers by the model, not by the reviewer). No tag for label/word disagreement.
VOCABULARY GAP: a detector firing on depicted faces (graffiti, a sculpted bust). About detection scope, not about a palette.
VOCABULARY GAP: an observation that text detection generalises across scripts. No axis for detector recall.

VOCABULARY GAP: the concept word "album-title" does not separate title from artist name; the reviewer reads it as "the main text". A naming/definition complaint about the question set, which no axis covers.

VOCABULARY GAP: feedback about the review rendering itself (three-layer mask overlay, confusing on first sight). The vocabulary describes palettes; it has no way to record a comment about the review instrument the reviewer is looking through.

VOCABULARY GAP: a definitional ruling about how to judge flat-vs-gradient ground (boundary softness is never the test). The gradient axis can only complain about a published gradient; there is no tag for a ruling about the criterion.
VOCABULARY GAP: same class as the previous entry — a canonical case fixing the continuous-progression vs discrete-areas axis. A criterion ruling, not a complaint about a palette.

VOCABULARY GAP: the reviewer says one artwork can legitimately support BOTH a valid flat palette and a valid gradient palette. The gradient axis is symmetric (should-be-flat / should-be-gradient) but has no way to say "both answers are defensible for this artwork" — meta/both-sides-good is the pairwise-verdict analogue and cannot be used for an artwork-level statement. Tagging either direction would be a contradiction of the text.
